newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says U.S. film case allegations 'groundless'.
newsitem.headline: Japan says U.S. film case allegations 'groundless'.

text.p: Japan Friday dismissed as "groundless" U.S. allegations that the Japanese government had attempted to thwart foreign entry into its photographic film and paper market.

"We believe that the U.S. allegations are groundless and all the alleged measures taken by the Japanese government are fully consistent with the GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) rules," Japan's Trade Ministry said.

The United States filed a complaint Thursday with a World Trade Organisation dispute settlement panel alleging that for the last 30 years Japan has imposed laws, regulations and administrative steps to strengthen its domestic industry and curtail opportunities for foreign firms.

"The government of Japan's intervention in re-ordering the conditions of competition in the photographic material industry has impaired market access for imports," U.S. Trade Representative designate Charlene Barshefsky told a news conference.
She said the effect of those measures was to nullify and impair the benefits Japan's trading partners expected from tariff concessions made in international trade agreements.
Barshefsky also said the case was not a fight between two competitors -- Eastman Kodak Co. and Fuji Photo Film Co. Ltd -- but a trade dispute between two countries.
"This is a case about classic protectionism accomplished through novel means," Barshefsky said.
Japan's Trade Ministry said it would analyse the specifics of the U.S. submission and rebut its factual and legal claims in accordance with WTO rules and procedures.

It said reports on Japan's distribution sector cited by the United States to support its case were "related to such issues as promoting modernisation of the distribution sector and do not contain any factor to treat imported film and paper unfavourably compared with domestic ones."
The ministry statement added: "Many of the alleged 'measures' are in fact reports of advisory councils ... and not government measures that the WTO panel can examine."
The ministry also denied a U.S. allegation that Japan's Large-Scale Retail Store Law limited the number of big retail stores and impeded sales opportunities for imported film.

Lawyers for Fuji Photo in Washington on Thursday also denied that the Japanese government had deliberately acted to thwart foreign competition and said U.S. trade officials had failed to prove their case.
The WTO, the successor to GATT, is not expected to reach a decision on the dispute until October.
